subject: Logging & redaction controls \u0014 follow-up and next steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>

Cc: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 30 Jul 2026 15:05:00 -0700
Subject: Logging & redaction controls  follow-up and next steps

Hi Alex / Priya 

Thanks again for a productive discovery call this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we stay aligned on scope for logging and sensitive-data redaction: 

Recap (what we heard)
- You need to retain request/response metadata for debugging but must ensure no PII is stored in logs.
- Compliance requirements: SOC 2 controls + 7-year retention policy for audit artifacts, but primary product logs should be retained no more than 365 days unless flagged.
- Concern about trace IDs / headers: teams want to correlate requests for support without exposing any customer-identifiable info.

Redaction & logging capabilities (high-level)
- Ingestion-time redaction: configurable detectors (PII regex + ML-based named-entity detection) to strip or mask PII from request bodies before it is persisted.
- Header controls: configurable allowlist/denylist for headers. Sensitive headers (Authorization, Cookie, X-User-Email) can be removed or masked.
- Trace IDs: options to hash/pseudonymize trace IDs (deterministic one-way hashing) or to encrypt under customer KMS (reversible only with customer key).
- Request/response logging: can be disabled per-route, sampled (e.g., 1%), or set to store only aggregated telemetry (latency, error rates).
- Retention: default 30/90/365-day buckets; support for customer-managed retention windows and archival to customer-owned storage for long-term retention.

Attached: redaction_controls_v1.pdf  outlines available knobs and recommended defaults for webhooks and chat endpoints.

Proposed next steps
1) Technical deep-dive with your engineering/security teams  propose Tue/Wed next week (I listed a couple of time slots below). We will include Dev Patel (solutions engineer) and Neha (security lead) from our side.
2) You share the SOC2 questionnaire and any sample logs (sanitized or production if you can) so we can map controls.
3) Well produce a short config proposal (per-route redaction + retention) and a non-prod runbook for testing.

Availability (PT): Tue 8/3 10:0011:00, Wed 8/4 14:0015:00  let me know what works or propose alternatives.

Thanks!
—
Marissa Cole
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.com | (415) 555-0142

Marissa 

Thanks for the clear recap. A couple quick clarifications before we set the deep-dive: 

- Trace IDs: do your redaction knobs preserve a form of the trace ID that lets us correlate logs across systems but removes any customer-identifiable tokens? We need to be able to link a support ticket to a request without exposing emails or account IDs.
- Headers: curious how granular the header denylist is  can we apply it per-client or per-route?
- Retention: for SOC 2 evidence we may need snapshots (audit artifacts) kept longer than 365 days. Is there a straightforward archival flow to our S3?

Attaching our SOC2 questionnaire  wed appreciate any early answers you can provide so we can prep our security/compliance reviewers.

Also, Wed 8/4 14:00 PT works for a technical call. Please include whoever owns KMS/encryption on your side.

Subject: Re: Logging & redaction controls  follow-up and next steps

Alex 

Appreciate the questions  answers below and a short plan for the Wed deep-dive: 

Trace IDs
- Option A (one-way pseudonymization): we apply a deterministic hash to trace IDs so they remain consistent across requests for correlation but do not reveal raw identifiers. This is the simplest approach and requires no key management.
- Option B (customer KMS reversible): we encrypt the trace ID using your KMS key so it can be decrypted by you for support/debugging. Good if you need reversible mapping under strict key controls.
- Option C (strip + replace): remove the trace ID and replace with a Redwood-generated UID (breaks cross-system correlation unless you map it externally).

Headers
- Denylist/allowlist is per-route and per-tenant. You can specify a global policy and exceptions for specific routes (for example, allow X-Request-ID but block X-User-Email).

Retention / archival
- We support configurable retention windows per-route and automatic archival to your S3 bucket for longer-term retention (preserves metadata only or full logs, based on policy). We can provide a template CloudFormation/IAM policy for the archival flow.

Security controls
- Redaction detectors: combination of regex-based masks and ML-based NER for names/emails/SSNs.
- Audit logs: admin actions and access to decrypted (KMS) values are logged and available for audit.

Attached: SOC2_evidence_request.xlsx  we filled the first tab with recommended settings and referenced controls where we can provide screenshots or exportable evidence.

Wed deep-dive (confirm): Wed 2026-08-04 14:00 PT. Agenda: 1) walk through sample logs and desired retention, 2) KMS/encryption options and IAM for archival, 3) demo of redaction rules and per-route config. Dev Patel will cover the redaction rule config snippets.

Next steps for us before the call:
- Alex/Priya: if possible, upload one or two representative request/response samples (sanitized) to the shared Drive link so we can prepare rule suggestions.
- Dev/Neha: well prepare a short demo (1013 min) that shows: ingestion redaction, header denylist, and deterministic hashing of a trace ID.

Thanks  looking forward to it.
—
Marissa
